question: What are the advantages of multiprocessor systems?
chapter: Unit 1 – Computer-System Architecture, OS Structure and Operations
reference_answer: Multiprocessor (parallel) systems give increased throughput, economy of scale, and increased reliability through graceful degradation or fault tolerance.
key_points: increased reliability / graceful degradation or fault tolerance

gold_quotes.quote: Increased throughput • Economy of scale • Increased reliability – graceful degradation or fault tolerance

question: How is symmetric multiprocessing different from asymmetric multiprocessing?
chapter: Unit 1 – Computer-System Architecture, OS Structure and Operations
reference_answer: In asymmetric multiprocessing each processor is assigned a specific task; in symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) every processor performs all tasks as peers, with no boss-worker relationship, sharing physical memory.
key_points: asymmetric: each processor has a specific task
symmetric: each processor performs all tasks
SMP processors are peers, no boss-worker relationship

gold_quotes.quote: Asymmetric Multiprocessing – each processor is assigned a specific task. 2. Symmetric Multiprocessing – each processor performs all tasks
In SMP all processors are peers; no boss– worker relationship exists between processors.

question: Why is putting two cores on one chip better than using two separate CPU chips?
chapter: Unit 1 – Computer-System Architecture, OS Structure and Operations
reference_answer: On-chip communication is faster than communication between chips, and one multicore chip uses significantly less power than several single-core chips.

gold_quotes.quote: on-chip communication is faster than between-chip communication
One chip with multiple cores uses significantly less power than multiple single-core chips

question: If my program gets stuck in an infinite loop, how does the OS stop it from using the CPU forever?
chapter: Unit 1 – Computer-System Architecture, OS Structure and Operations
reference_answer: The OS sets a timer (a counter decremented on each clock tick) that interrupts the computer after a specified period; when it reaches zero an interrupt occurs and the OS can terminate the program.
key_points: timer interrupt after a specified period
OS regains control and can terminate the program

gold_quotes.quote: Timer can be used to prevent a user program from running too long (terminate the program)
When counter reaches zero, an interrupt occurs
Other process problems include infinite loop

question: What happens to the mode bit when a user program makes a system call, and what happens when the call returns?
chapter: Unit 1 – Computer-System Architecture, OS Structure and Operations
reference_answer: A system call (trap) switches the hardware from user mode to kernel mode by setting the mode bit to 0; when the request is fulfilled the system sets the mode bit back to 1 (user mode) before returning control to the user program.
key_points: system call switches to kernel mode
mode bit set to 0 in kernel mode
mode bit set back to 1 (user mode) before returning

gold_quotes.quote: System call changes mode to kernel, return from call resets it to user
hardware switches from user mode to kernel mode (changes the state of the mode bit to 0)

question: What is the difference between multiprogramming and multitasking?
chapter: Unit 1 – Computer-System Architecture, OS Structure and Operations
reference_answer: Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory so the CPU always has one to execute, switching when a job waits (e.g. for I/O). Multitasking (time sharing) switches between jobs so frequently that users can interact with each job while it runs, giving response times under a second.
key_points: multiprogramming: CPU always has a job, switches when a job waits
multitasking: switches so often that users interact with each job

gold_quotes.quote: Multiprogramming organizes jobs (code and data) so CPU always has one to execute
CPU switches jobs so frequently that users can interact with each job while it is running

question: How can the OS keep track of which disk blocks are free without using much memory?
chapter: Unit 1 – Kernel Data Structures and Computing Environments
reference_answer: With a bitmap: a string of n binary digits where each bit gives the status of one resource (0 = available, 1 = unavailable). It is commonly used for large numbers of resources such as disk blocks.

gold_quotes.quote: Bitmap - string of n binary digits representing the status of n items
Commonly used to represent the availability of a large number of resources (disk blocks)

question: Why does the operating system use a stack when a function is called?
chapter: Unit 1 – Kernel Data Structures and Computing Environments
reference_answer: A stack is LIFO: when a function is called its parameters, local variables and return address are pushed onto the stack, and returning from the call pops them off.
key_points: parameters, local variables and return address pushed on call

gold_quotes.quote: Parameters, local variables and the return address are pushed onto the stack when a function is called

question: Which data structure does Linux use to decide which task runs next?
chapter: Unit 1 – Kernel Data Structures and Computing Environments
reference_answer: A balanced binary search tree, which has O(log n) search performance.

gold_quotes.quote: Balanced binary search tree – (a tree containing n items has at most log n levels)
Used by Linux for selecting which task to run next (CPU-Scheduling algorithm)

question: How is peer-to-peer computing different from client-server computing?
chapter: Unit 1 – Kernel Data Structures and Computing Environments
reference_answer: In client-server computing, servers respond to requests generated by clients. Peer-to-peer does not distinguish clients and servers: every node is a peer that can act as client, server or both.
key_points: P2P: no distinction between clients and servers
each node can be client, server or both

gold_quotes.quote: P2P does not distinguish clients and servers
Many systems now servers, responding to requests generated by clients

question: What is the difference between SaaS, PaaS and IaaS?
chapter: Unit 1 – Kernel Data Structures and Computing Environments
reference_answer: SaaS provides applications over the Internet (e.g. a word processor); PaaS provides a software stack ready for application use (e.g. a database server); IaaS provides servers or storage over the Internet (e.g. storage for backup).

gold_quotes.quote: Software as a Service (SaaS) – one or more applications available via the Internet
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) – servers or storage available over Internet
Delivers computing, storage, even apps as a service across a network

question: What makes a real-time operating system different from a normal one?
chapter: Unit 1 – Kernel Data Structures and Computing Environments
reference_answer: A real-time OS has well-defined, fixed time constraints: processing must be done within the constraint, and the system operates correctly only if the constraints are met.
key_points: processing must finish within the constraint
correct only if constraints are met

gold_quotes.quote: Real-time OS has well-defined fixed time constraints

question: After a program starts an I/O operation, what are the two ways control can return to the user program?
reference_answer: Either control returns only when the I/O completes (the CPU idles with a wait instruction or loop, and only one I/O request is outstanding), or control returns immediately without waiting, and the program uses a system call to wait for completion while the OS tracks devices in a device-status table.
key_points: return only after I/O completes (wait instruction / loop)
system call to wait; device-status table

gold_quotes.quote: After I/O starts, control returns to user program only upon I/O completion
After I/O starts, control returns to user program without waiting for I/O completion
